Aromaticity-Driven Access to Cycloalkyl-Fused Naphthalenes
Karekar Sanjeev, § Silver Raju, § and Srivari Chandrasekhar *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 4013 −4017 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: We report the e ﬃcient synthesis of cycloalkyl-fused naphthalenes through the [4 + 2]-cycloaddtion/decarboxylative
aromatization of alkyne-tethered aryne insertion adducts. These sca ﬀolds were di ﬃcult to synthesize using conventional reactions.
The reaction proceeds via the formation of a benzopyrylium intermediate followed by intramolecular [4 + 2] cycloaddition and a
subsequent decarboxylation pathway. This method is also compatible with allene-tethered substrates to a ﬀord similar products. In
addition, the one-pot synthesis of polysubstituted naphthalenes via aryne insertion/benzannulation has also been developed in good
yield.
T
he construction of aromatic architectures with prede ﬁned
substitutions is an important area of research. 1 Polycyclic
aromatic compounds have useful applications in material
science.
2 Naphthalene chemistry has played a pivotal role in
asymmetric catalysis. 3 The Naphtha byproducts of petroleum
reﬁnery have become the useful starting materials in this
research activity. The [4 + 2] cycloaddition is most sought-
after reaction to annulate the existing benzene rings. 4 These
cycloaddition reactions need a standard diene/dienophile with
a favorable electronic con ﬁguration. The benzannulation
reactions are reported involving transition-metal catalysis,
5
Lewis acid catalysis, 6 and thermal cycloadditions. 7
Benzannulation to construct substituted naphthalenes could
provide varied substitutions (mono, di, tri, etc.) based on the
reactants.
8 Our group has been expanding the scope and
applications of Stoltz’s cycloaddition−fragmentation process to
natural product synthesis and toward medicinally relevant
bioactives.9 Stoltz’s process is basically the addition of a β-keto
ester to an in-situ-generated benzyne to realize an ortho-
disubstituted benzene with a carbonyl group and a methylene
ester taking the ortho positions to each other (acyl-phenyl
acetic acid derivatives).
10 We anticipated that an appropriate
substitution on the C-2 position of the β-keto ester having an
alkyne group (pentyne or hexyne) would trigger a Conia-Ene
process followed by a cascade of reactions to provide a
functionalized tricyclic framework.
The study was initiated by the cyclization of 3a (readily
synthesized from acyl alkylation of the benzyne precursor 1a
with β-ketoester 2a) in the presence of BF 3·Et2O (1.5 equiv) in
1,2-dichloroethane (DCE) at 80 °C for 2 h to provide the
product 4a in 85% yield ( Scheme 1 ). The product 4a was
conﬁrmed by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrosco-
py and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) analysis. 11
Instead of alicyclic rings (two) being stitched ( 4ab) via the
Conia-Ene product 4aa, we observed a clean naphthyl-fused
cyclopentane 4a via [4 + 2]-cycloaddition in decent yield. With
this initial observation, we screened the annulation reaction
with a catalytic amount of various Lewis acids including BF
3·
Et2O( s e et h e Supporting Information for details) and
obtained 0 to <10% of product; in most cases, the starting
material was recovered. Among all veri ﬁed reaction conditions,
1.5 equiv of BF
3·OEt2 in DCE at 80 °C for 2 h provided the
best yield.
With the optimized conditions in hand, we then explored
the substrate scope with various alkyne-tethered aryl ketones 3,
and the results are summarized in Scheme 2 . Initially, the
reaction was carried out with pentyne-tethered aryl ketones,
where R
1 is an alkyl, aryl, or naphthyl, giving the corresponding

cyclopentane-fused naphthalenes 4a−4g in good to excellent
yields. It is interesting to note that the methyl-substituted
alkyne was also well tolerated in the reaction (entries 4c, 4i,
and 4j). The [4 + 2]-cycloaddition of hexyne-tethered aryl
ketones also furnished the corresponding fused cyclohexane
products 4h−4l in 53 −91% yield. For the O-tethered alkyne,
where R
1 was Me, the reaction proceeded well to o ﬀer the
annulation product 4m in 74% yield. When R 1 was a methyl
and R 2 was a phenyl, the reaction proceeded to give the
cyclized product 4n in 10% yield. Unfortunately, further
attempts to synthesize four- and seven-membered ring- fused
naphthalenes were not successful.
Our next task was to explore the intramolecular [4 + 2]-
benzannulation with allene-tethered aryl ketones. Initially,
allene 5l was subjected to standard reaction condition to give a
mixture of cyclohexane- and cyclopentane-fused products 4l
and 4l′ in a 1.3:1 ratio as an inseparable mixture in 52% overall
yield ( Scheme 3 ). The same reaction at room temperature
exclusively a ﬀorded the cyclohexane-fused product 4l in 53%
yield. Steric hindrance is the determining factor behind the
observed regioselectivity for the allene terminal double bond.
Various allenes 5 with di ﬀerent aryl and alkyl substituents at
the 1-phenyl ketone proved to be suitable substrates for the
annulation reaction at room temperature to give the
corresponding products ( 4h, 4l, 4o, 4p, and 4q), albeit in
moderate yield ( Scheme 4 ).
Next, we explored the scope of alkene-tethered aryl ketones
6 in [4 + 2]-benzannulation under the standard reaction
conditions at 80 °C( Scheme 5 ). To our delight, hexene-
tethered substrates gave the corresponding naphthalenes 4h
and 4p in moderate yield. However, in the case of pentene-
tethered substrates, we observed only trace amount of products
(entries 4a and 4b).
Enticed by the previously described experimental result, we
attempted the one-pot aryne insertion/benzannulation reac-
tion between the aryne precursor and the alkyne-tethered β-
keto ester by the sequential addition of reagents ( Scheme 6 ).
Initially, tri ﬂate 1 and β-ketoester 2 were treated with CsF (3
equiv) in tetrahydrofuran (THF) solvent at 60 °C for 6 h.
After completion of the insertion reaction (monitored by thin
layer chromatography (TLC)), the excess CsF was quenched
with the addition of Amberlite IR120 H until the reaction
mixture became acidic; then, the reaction mixture was ﬁltered
and evaporated under reduced pressure. The crude product
was dissolved in DCE; then, BF
3·Et2O (1.5 equiv) was added,
and the reaction was continued at 80 °C for 2 h. To our
satisfaction, we were able to isolate the required products in
moderate to good yields, as shown in Scheme 6 .
On the basis of the above experimental results and previous
reports, a plausible reaction pathway is proposed in Scheme 7.
The reaction might be initiated by the activation of alkyne 3 or
allene 5 (A) with Lewis acid to form the hemiketal

intermediate B. The elimination of the hydroxyl group from
intermediate B aﬀords the highly reactive benzopyrylium
intermediate C, which readily undergoes intramolecular [4 +
2] cycloaddition to give the bridged intermediate D followed
by decarboxylation to produce the required naphthalene
product 4. In the case of alkene 6, intermediate D′ undergoes
ring-opening via β-H elimination
11 to give intermediate E
followed by acid-mediated decarboxylation/oxidation 12 to
provide the desired aromatized product 4.
In conclusion, we have developed the Lewis-acid-catalyzed
intramolecular [4 + 2]-cycloaddition/aromatization of alkyne-,
allene-, and alkene-tethered aryne insertion adducts to access
cycloalkyl-fused naphthalenes. The reaction pathway involves
the formation of a benzopyrylium intermediate followed by
intramolecular [4 + 2] cycloaddition and subsequent
decarboxylation. In addition, a one-pot aryne insertion/
benzannulation reaction has also been developed in good yield.
